# Troubleshooting
Source: https://docs.crowdedkingdoms.com/unreal-sdk/exec/troubleshooting

# Troubleshooting

:::note
Server Objects run on [ck-exec](/exec/intro).
:::

This page is for Blueprint and C++ alike. In Blueprint, **Get Status** and **Get Failure Reason** are the nodes for what `GetStatus()` and `GetFailureReason()` answer in C++, and **On Failed** carries the **Outcome**, **Reason**, **Retryable** and **Code** that `OnDone` receives. On a **Call** node those pins are in the advanced area: click the small arrow at the bottom of the node to show them. **Code** is filled only by a [Game Kit starter](./use-game-kit-starters.md#refusals-and-their-codes).

## A Server Object does not become Ready

Read its status first; the four statuses are on [Get a Server Object](./from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md#status). Then the reason it gives.

### Waiting is not failing

Most problems on the server clear up by themselves, so reading and watching a Server Object recover from every temporary one without your help. Before its first values arrive, a Server Object waits them out in **Connecting** instead of failing. It keeps trying, a little less often each time and, unless the server asks for longer, never more than 15 seconds apart, and becomes Ready on its own once the cause is gone. Every wait before a retry or a redial is stretched by a random amount, up to half again: a failed read's first retry waits 1 to 1.5 seconds, and a lost connection is redialled after 1 to 1.5 seconds, then 2 to 3, and so on up to 30 to 45. So many players do not retry in step after a server restart. While it waits, `GetFailureReason()` says what it is waiting for. It waits when:

- the type is not deployed on the server yet, or the app now runs an older version without it: the reason reads "`village_beacon` is not deployed on the server";
- the type is switched off on the server, or the whole app is switched off or paused (by its owner, or because it ran out of funds): the reason reads "The server is switched off or paused, so this Server Object waits: " followed by the platform's own words, such as "`village_beacon` is switched off in app 456" or "app 456 is switched off". It reads the same whether the server says so with its pause and switch-off statuses (`AppPaused`, `AppDisabled`, `TypeDisabled`) or, on an older server, with a refusal in words, and a read made while the connection is redialling into a paused or switched-off app shows this reason too. To show the player a message instead of retrying, see [When the app is paused](../services/authentication.md#when-the-app-is-paused);
- the server does not let players use the type;
- the server code crashed and its Server Object is restarting;
- the server did not answer in time, or failed internally;
- the server code refused the read, such as `unreadable` when the state holds a value players cannot read (see [refusals from your server code](#refusals-from-your-server-code));
- the server is busy or cannot be reached; when the platform could not start the Server Object to read it, for example because the app is at its instance or memory limit, the reason reads "The server could not be reached: " followed by the platform's words;
- the connection to the server could not be opened: the reason reads "Could not open the connection to the server for `<Type Name>`: " followed by why, and names the type the SDK tried it with. When the refusal is that the server is switched off or paused, its error ending in `(APP_PAUSED)`, `(APP_DISABLED)` or `(TYPE_DISABLED)`, or saying so in words on an older server, it reads "The server is switched off or paused for `<Type Name>`: " followed by the error instead. A try made with the root or a Server Function Library names no type, since the platform is not told one: "Could not open the connection to the server: " or "The server is switched off or paused: ". The next try uses another type's Server Object, so one type that is not deployed or is switched off does not hold up the others.

So a game can acquire its Server Objects before their server code is deployed, and they come up as soon as it is.

### What makes it fail

A Server Object moves to **Failed**, and stays there, only when waiting cannot help:

- this player may not read it: an [Owner Only](./from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md#owner-only-types) Server Object that belongs to someone else, or a [Game Kit starter](./use-game-kit-starters.md) that refused the read with a code, such as "The server code for session refused to let this player read it (forbidden): ..." (a starter's `cooldown` or `unavailable` is waited out instead);
- the deployed server code does not serve the variables players can see, or was built for another version of the SDK: generate and deploy it again;
- the values the server sends do not match the definition's State struct: the definition and the deployed code are out of step, so generate and deploy again;
- the server refused the SDK's request as malformed;
- the Game API named a Server Object gateway outside its own domains, so the SDK will not connect to it: the reason reads "Could not open the connection to the server: the Game API named a gateway outside its own domains (" followed by why and "); if you host the server yourself, add its domain to Allowed Exec Gateway Domains in Project Settings". It is not retried until you acquire an object again (or call Restart). See [Server Object gateway domains](../reference/project-settings.md#server-object-gateway-domains) for the setting;
- the player signed out (`The player signed out`);
- the player's access to the game ended (`Your access ended: ` followed by the reason); see [When access ends](#when-access-ends).

To try again after a failure, call `Acquire` again with the same definition and Instance Id, from the same owner or another; in Blueprint, call **Rejoin** on the component. The same object starts over from Connecting, and its values start from the definition's defaults.

### When access ends

A player's access to the game can end while they play: it is suspended, revoked or expired, the platform signs the player out, or the account is blocked. The Game Session fires **On Access Ended** (see [When the player's access ends](../services/authentication.md#when-the-players-access-ends)) and Server Objects stop:

- Every Server Object fails with `Your access ended: ` followed by the reason, whatever its status was.
- A call in flight, and every call made afterwards, finishes as the outcome **Access Ended** (`ECrowdyServerCallOutcome::AccessEnded`), with the same reason. It is not retryable.
- Nothing reconnects or retries by itself, since the server would refuse it.

Show the reason and send the player back to sign in. A successful sign-in clears the ended state: a **Crowdy Server Object** component and a typed node set to **Find By Asset** get their Server Object again on their own. Code that called `Acquire` itself calls it again.

## A value is not what you expect

- **A newer server sends an enum value this build does not have.** The field keeps its default and the SDK logs a warning once, under `LogCrowdyExec`. Update the game, or keep the value's old name under **Enum Value Names** if it was a rename.
- **The connection dropped.** Changes made while it was gone are not replayed. The SDK reads the values again when it reconnects and reports the fields that differ as one change. See [Get a Server Object](./from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md#sign-out-shutdown-and-dropped-connections).
- **The values stopped changing, or never arrived.** Check `GetStatus()` and `GetFailureReason()`. A Server Object waiting in Connecting (its type not deployed yet, or switched off) or one that has Failed keeps the last values it had, and the reason says what it is waiting for or why it stopped. See [Status](./from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md#status).

## A message never arrives

A [message](./create-a-type.md#server-messages) is heard once, when the server sends it, and nothing keeps it. When a game or a Server Object expects one and gets nothing, check these in order.

**In a game, from Blueprint or C++:**

- **Players Can Listen is off.** Only the server code of a type that Listens To this one hears the message. A Blueprint **Received** node for it does not compile ("heard only by other Server Object types; turn on Players Can Listen"), and **Watch Message** or `WatchMessage` logs "... is heard only by other Server Object types; turn on Players Can Listen to hear it in a game" once and does nothing. Tick it in the asset, then generate and deploy the type. Likewise a name the definition does not have logs "... has no message named ..., so nothing can listen to it".
- **The deployed server does not send it yet.** A message you added, renamed or changed reaches the server only with the generated code and a deploy; see [After you change the definition](./write-server-logic.md#after-you-change-the-definition).
- **The function that sends it did not succeed.** A message is published only when the function that sent it succeeds, after its changes. A refusal sends nothing; look at the caller's `Reason` and the server code's [logs](./deploy-with-server-compute.md).
- **The game was not listening at that moment.** A message sent before the game started listening, or while its connection was closed, is lost and never replayed. Check `GetStatus()`: a Server Object that is not Ready announces nothing, and a message that arrives while it is still reading its values is held and announced once they are current, at most 32 of them. Past 32 the oldest is dropped and the log warns "held back 32 messages while reading its values, so the oldest was dropped".
- **The platform refused to let the player listen.** The log warns once, "`<Type Name>` could not listen to its `<Message>` message, so it is asked again after a wait: " followed by the platform's reason. The SDK asks again after a wait that grows from 1 second to 30, and nothing else about the Server Object fails. A message sent while the listen is refused is lost.
- **A limit was reached.** A connection allows 256 subscriptions, and each time the game listens it counts against the 120 calls a connection may make every 10 seconds. Each message a game listens to on each Server Object is one subscription, so many objects with several messages each can reach it: give back the objects the game no longer needs, and listen only to the messages it uses.
- **The message comes before the change it follows.** A type that keeps [a record per entity](./keep-a-record-per-entity.md) sends its records in batches, so a message sent right after a record changed can arrive first. Put what the listener needs into the payload.
- **The payload does not fit its struct.** The message is dropped with a warning that names it. The definition and the deployed code are out of step: generate and deploy again.

**In server code, listening to another type:**

- **The listen was never applied.** A `listen::...` call takes effect only when the function that made it succeeds, and the function fails, with `could not listen to boss.boss_defeated:` and the reason, when the platform refuses it. A type can listen to 256 messages at once. Check the function's result.
- **The key is not the sender's.** The key is the sender's Instance Id, with capitals significant: `boss-1` and `Boss-1` are two Server Objects.
- **The sender is not in Listen To.** Without it the `listen` functions and the `on_<type>_<message>` handler do not exist; see [Listen to a message](./write-server-logic.md#listen-to-a-message). Generate and deploy after adding it.
- **The message was sent too early.** One sent before the listen was applied, or while the listener was stopped, is missed.
- **The handler failed.** A handler that returns an error puts its state back, and a payload it cannot read fails it with `bad_message: <type>.<message>: ...`; read the logs.

## Outcomes

`Outcome` is an `ECrowdyServerCallOutcome`. The platform's own status is in brackets.

| Outcome | What happened | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Success [`Ok`] | The server code ran and answered. `Reply` holds the outputs. | Nothing. The watched values change for everyone, you included. |
| ServerError [`AppError`, `Internal`] | The server code refused the call or failed, or the platform failed handling it. `Reason` carries the message. Also returned when the reply does not fit the function's outputs. | Show or log `Reason`. See [refusals from your server code](#refusals-from-your-server-code). |
| Busy [`Busy`, `RateLimited`] | The server stayed busy through every retry. | Try again later, and call less often. If one Server Object takes many calls at once, raise **Calls Waiting** in the type's [Server Limits](./create-a-type.md#every-setting). |
| Unavailable [`Unavailable`, `Moved`] | The server could not be reached, so the call may or may not have run; or the Server Object has Failed (`Reason` is its failure reason). When the platform says why, such as the app being at its instance limit, `Reason` adds its words after "The server could not be reached:". Not retried by the SDK. A Game Kit starter's `unavailable` refusal (another hub the call needed did not answer) arrives as Unavailable too, with **Code** `unavailable` and `bRetryable` set. | Check `GetStatus()`. Call again only if running the function twice is harmless, or after the watched values show it did not happen. |
| NotDeployed [`NotFound`] | This type is not deployed on the server. The Server Object itself waits in Connecting until it is. | Deploy the type's server code to the app. |
| Timeout [`DeadlineExceeded`] | Nobody answered in time, and `Reason` says which side gave up. "AttackBoss ran past its Time per Call on the server: handler exceeded its deadline" means the server's own limit stopped the call (the type's **Time per Call**, 2 seconds unless changed), followed by the server's message; for a read it reads "The server took longer than this type's Time per Call to read this Server Object" (or "watch"). "The server sent no answer in time; the connection may be slow or lost" means no answer reached the game within the project's **Server Object Call Timeout** (20 seconds unless changed; see [Project settings](../reference/project-settings.md#server-object-timeouts)): the longest **Time per Call** (10 seconds) plus time spent waiting behind other calls on the server. "No answer within 5 seconds; FeedBeacon may still have run on the server" means the call's own **Timeout** ran out first (5 seconds here); it is not retryable, and an answer that arrives later is not reported. The call may or may not have taken effect. A call past **Time per Call** also restarts that Server Object from its last save, so changes since the last save are lost. | Watch the values before you call again. If the function does real work that needs longer, raise **Time per Call** in the type's [Server Limits](./create-a-type.md#every-setting); otherwise keep functions short, and set **Save Every** low on a type whose recent changes matter. **Time per Call** counts the function only, not the time a call waits behind others. A call that gives up earlier than the project's timeout has a **Timeout** set on its Call node (`TimeoutSeconds` in C++); clear it, or raise it, if the server needs longer. |
| Denied [`Denied`] | The server refused the call. Either the platform refused it, because players may not call this type at all, and `Reason` reads "The server refused the call to Feed: " followed by the platform's words; or the type's own server code refused the player by a rule in the asset, such as **Callable By**, **Owner Only** or a **Cooldown**, and `Reason` says why. A Game Kit starter's `forbidden` and `cooldown` refusals arrive as Denied too, with **Code** set and the starter's words in `Reason`; `cooldown` is `bRetryable`. A call refused because the server is switched off or paused is [Paused](#outcomes), not Denied. | Show `Reason`. A refusal by a rule stays a refusal until something changes, except a cooldown, which is `bRetryable`: call again after the seconds it names. See [refusals from your server code](#refusals-from-your-server-code). |
| Paused [`AppPaused`, `AppDisabled`, `TypeDisabled`; `Denied` in words from an older server] | The game's server, or this type, is switched off or paused, by its owner or because the app ran out of funds. The platform says which with its own status: `AppPaused` for an app paused by billing, `AppDisabled` for the whole app switched off, `TypeDisabled` for one type switched off. A server from before those statuses refuses with `Denied` and says so in words, and the SDK reads that as Paused too. It is retryable, and `Reason` reads "The server is switched off or paused, so it refused the call to Feed: " followed by the platform's words, such as "`village_beacon` is switched off in app 456", "app 456 is switched off" or "app 456 is paused: ...". A call that got no answer because the connection was redialling into a paused or switched-off app reports Paused with the platform's words too, not Timeout. | Try again later, or show the player a paused message; see [When the app is paused](../services/authentication.md#when-the-app-is-paused). Code that only checked for Denied should handle Paused too, and a Blueprint Switch on the outcome has a **Paused** pin. |
| AccessEnded | The player's access to the game ended: suspended, revoked, expired, signed out by the platform, or the account blocked. `Reason` reads `Your access ended: ` followed by why. Not retryable, and it applies to every Server Object until the player signs in again. | Show `Reason` and return the player to sign in; see [When access ends](#when-access-ends). A Blueprint Switch on the outcome has an **Access Ended** pin. |
| Refused [`AppError` with a Game Kit code] | A [Game Kit starter](./use-game-kit-starters.md#refusals-and-their-codes) refused the call for a reason of the game's, such as a full match (`full`) or another player's turn (`not_your_turn`). **Code** (`Code` in C++) holds the code and `Reason` the starter's words. Not retryable. Your own types never answer Refused. | Branch on **Code**, and show `Reason`. The codes are on the platform's [Refusals carry a code](/game-kit/protocol#refusals-carry-a-code). A Blueprint Switch on the outcome has a **Refused** pin. |
| ServerCrashed [`Trapped`] | The server code crashed handling the call. The Server Object restarts on the server from its last save, so its most recent changes may be lost; the SDK reads its values again and reports what differs. | Read the server code's log. |
| BadRequest [`BadRequest`] | The call could not be sent as asked: an unknown function name, params of the wrong struct, or params that could not be encoded. `Reason` says which. | Fix the call. |
| Canceled | The Server Object was given back, or the player signed out, before the call finished. | Nothing, usually; the owner is gone or the session ended. |

## Refusals from your server code

A refusal whose message starts with one of these words came from the [server code generated for the type](./write-server-logic.md#what-the-generated-code-does-for-you), not from your own logic:

- `unknown_method`: the deployed server code has no such function. The definition is newer than what is deployed; generate and deploy the server code again. It reaches `OnDone` as a `ServerError`.
- `denied`: a player called a function they may not: **Server Only**, **Members** or **Leader** without being one, or, on an Owner Only type, a Server Object that is not theirs. It reaches `OnDone` as `Denied`, and `Reason` is the text after the word, such as "only members may call Deposit". A Server Only function is one no player may call, so a call from a game client is refused this way every time; only other server code and developer tools can call it. Set it back to **Players** in the [definition asset](./create-a-type.md#callable-by) if players should be able to. Deploy the type again afterwards, since the server code carries the choice.
- `cooldown`: the player called a function inside its **Cooldown**. It reaches `OnDone` as `Denied` with `bRetryable` set, and `Reason` says how many seconds to wait, such as "Feed can be called again in 4 s".
- `bad_params`: the server could not read the params, or a number is outside its **Value Range** (`bad_params: Amount must be 1 to 100`), and the rest of the reason names the field. Usually the deployed code is older than the definition. It reaches `OnDone` as a `ServerError`.
- `unreadable`: the Server Object's state holds a value no Unreal client could read, such as text in an `FGuid` field that is not a GUID, often one loaded from a save that older server code made. The rest of the reason names the field, such as `unreadable: Id: the server state holds a value players cannot read: a GUID is not in a form Unreal reads`. Reads are refused until your server code replaces the value, so players' Server Objects wait in Connecting with this as their reason and become Ready by themselves once it is fixed. See [the values every client can read](./write-server-logic.md#what-the-generated-code-does-for-you).
- `bad_seed`: the starting values given to a new Server Object hold a value no Unreal client could read, and the rest of the reason names the field. The Server Object does not start.
- `the change was not kept`: the call or hook would have put such a value into a watched field, or the reply held one, or a message it sent held one or was larger than 1 MiB, so the state went back to what it was. It reaches `OnDone` as a `ServerError`.
- `bad_message`: a message this type listens to could not be read as its payload, as in `bad_message: boss.boss_defeated: ...`. The handler fails and the state goes back; the sender's definition and this type's deployed code are out of step, so generate and deploy both again.

The [full list of what a refused player sees](./access-members-and-timers.md#what-a-refused-player-sees) is on the members page.

Any other `ServerError` reason is the message your server code refused with, such as the beacon saying it is full.

## A call to a library from server code fails

The first call to a [Server Function Library](./server-function-libraries.md) after it has been idle can take over a second. A player's game just waits for it. A Server Object's function that calls the library is held to the platform's call deadline, and a call that outlasts it fails with "call deadline passed" although the library may still finish. A boss that rolls loot when it falls sees it as `loot_roller.roll_loot failed: call deadline passed`.

- **Decide what a failed call means.** If the answer is optional, as a drop is, take it only when the call came back: `if let Ok(loot) = calls::loot_roller::roll_loot(ctx, &roll) { ... }`, as in [Loot for the Hollow Giant](./examples/hollow-giant-loot.md#the-boss-rolls-on-its-fall).
- **Call again once when the function is safe to repeat.** A pure calculation is. The second call finds the library warm:

  ```rust
  let loot = calls::loot_roller::roll_loot(ctx, &roll).or_else(|_| calls::loot_roller::roll_loot(ctx, &roll))?;
  ```

  Do not repeat a call that changes a Server Object unless repeating it is harmless; see [Call other Server Objects](./access-members-and-timers.md#call-other-server-objects).
- **The helper does not exist.** `calls::loot_roller` is made only when the caller lists the library under **Can Call**, or the caller uses `calls::any` with **Can Call Any Type**. Add it, generate the caller's server code and deploy again.
- **`app N has no node type`.** A call by `calls::any` named a type the app does not run, or misspelled it. Deploy does not check names given to `calls::any`.
- **`denied`.** A player called a function that is **Server Only** ("players may not call this function") or **Developers Only** ("only developer tools may call this function"). Other server code can call a Server Only one, and developer tools both; see [Callable By](./create-a-type.md#callable-by).
- **Unavailable, with the platform's words.** The app is at its limit on running Server Objects, and every instance of the library counts toward it; see [Scaling](./server-function-libraries.md#scaling).

A function that sees a value reset between two calls is working as designed: a library keeps nothing, and each instance runs several copies of your code with their own memory. Keep the value in a Server Object.

## Library calls time out during a burst

A burst of calls that each keep the processor busy, such as many loot rolls at once, can come back as **Timeout** with "ran past its Time per Call on the server", even though one call alone is quick. The calls an instance runs at the same time share its processor, and **Time per Call** counts the time that passes, not the work done. The platform adds an instance only after calls have waited 2 seconds, so the first moments of a burst all land on the instances already running. In a test with one instance running four calls at once, 300 ms of work per call, and two players each sending 24 at once, a Time per Call of 2000 ms failed some calls and 5000 ms answered all of them.

- **Give the function room.** Raise **Time per Call** to cover **Parallel Calls per Instance** times the work one call does.
- **Start with more instances.** Raise **Min Instances** when bursts are expected, such as when a round ends and every player opens a chest.
- **Run fewer at once per instance.** A lower **Parallel Calls per Instance** gives each call more of the processor; raise **Max Instances** to keep the total.

## A Server Function Library will not save

Saving shows these for a library, and they are the whole list besides the usual checks of its Type Name, functions and server names:

| Message | What to do |
|---|---|
| "RollLoot: Members and Leader need members, and a Server Function Library has none." | Set the function's **Callable By** to **Players**, **Server Only** or **Developers Only**. |
| "RollLoot: a cooldown is saved data, and a Server Function Library saves none." | Set its **Cooldown** to 0. To limit how often a player may call, put the function on a Server Object. |
| "Max Instances must be at least Min Instances." | Raise **Max Instances**, or lower **Min Instances**. They are under **Scaling**. |
| "loot_roller is a Server Function Library and sends no messages." | A Server Object lists the library under **Listen To**. Move it to **Can Call**. |

See [Checks when you save](./server-function-libraries.md#checks-when-you-save).

## A ping fails

**Ping Server Objects** (`UCrowdyServerObjectSubsystem::Ping` in C++) fails with a `Reason` instead of a round trip when:

- "No Server Object connection is open": a ping never opens a connection. Acquire a Server Object first and ping once it is Ready, or ping again after the connection comes back.
- "Too many pings: the platform answers at most 60 every 10 seconds": the platform drops the rest of a connection's pings without a word, so the SDK refuses them before sending. Ping on a timer of a second or more, not every frame.

See [Ping the platform](./from-blueprint/call-functions.md#ping-the-platform).

## Seeing what a Server Object is doing

When a Server Object never becomes Ready, stops changing, or two players disagree about it, turn on `crowdy.exec.trace`. It is off by default, and the warnings and errors print whether it is on or not. Turn it on in the editor's console (press the backtick key, in Play In Editor too):

```text
crowdy.exec.trace 1
```

or, for a packaged game or an editor started from the command line, add this to the command line:

```text
-ini:Engine:[ConsoleVariables]:crowdy.exec.trace=1
```

The lines go to the Output Log under `LogCrowdyExec`, at Log verbosity, each starting with `exec:`, then the type and Instance Id (`boss/boss-1`). An [Owner Only](./from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md#owner-only-types) Server Object prints `owner` in place of the Instance Id, so the player's user id never reaches the log. The Players Online root has no Instance Id, so it prints `-` in its place, such as `exec: root/- read applied ...`. For a shared boss being hit by two players, one player's log reads:

```text
exec: boss/boss-1 status Connecting -> Ready
exec: boss/boss-1 subscribe ok
exec: boss/boss-1 read applied epoch=3 seq=41 changed=Health,MaxHealth,Phase,Respawns,Hits,LastHitBy
exec: boss/boss-1 call Hit sent
exec: boss/boss-1 push applied epoch=3 seq=42 changed=Health,Hits,LastHitBy
exec: boss/boss-1 call Hit answered Success ms=63
exec: boss/boss-1 push applied epoch=3 seq=43 changed=Health,Phase,Hits,LastHitBy
exec: boss/boss-1 push stale epoch=3 seq=43
exec: boss/boss-1 call Hit sent
exec: boss/boss-1 call Hit answered Denied ms=41
exec: connection closed
exec: redial ok
exec: boss/boss-1 reread reason=reconnect
exec: boss/boss-1 read applied epoch=3 seq=47 changed=Health,Hits,LastHitBy
```

What it prints:

- **Status changes**, such as `status Connecting -> Ready`.
- **Every read and push that was applied**, with its `epoch`, its `seq` and the names of the variables that changed (`changed=-` when none did). The `epoch` changes when the server restarts the Server Object, and `seq` orders its changes. The `seq` printed is the one the SDK applied, so if two players' logs show the same `epoch` and `seq` lines, they saw the same changes. The names come in the order Watch Variables reports them. A push that is older than what the object already has prints `push stale`, with the object's current `epoch` and `seq`, and is not applied.
- **Why it read again**, as `reread reason=` followed by `gap` (a change was missed), `overflow` (so many changes arrived while a read was in flight that they could not all be held), `epoch` (the server restarted the object), `reconnect` (the connection came back) or `ownerOnly` (an [Owner Only](./from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md#owner-only-types) or Members type, which tells watchers to read instead of sending the values).
- **Subscribes**, as `subscribe ok` or `subscribe failed` followed by the reason.
- **Calls**: `call Hit sent`, and `call Hit answered` with the [outcome](#outcomes) and how many milliseconds the answer took. A call the SDK retries for you because the server was busy prints `sent` once.
- **Connection**: `exec: dial failed` with the reason when the first connection could not be made, `exec: connection closed` when an open one drops, then `exec: redial ok` or `exec: redial failed` with the reason. Every `redial ok` is preceded by a `connection closed`. A close on purpose names why, and no redial follows it: `exec: connection closed (no Server Object in use)`, `(signed out)` or `(shutting down)`. The next Server Object you get opens a fresh connection.

It prints the names of the variables that changed, never their values, and never a token. Turn it off again with `crowdy.exec.trace 0` once you have your answer, since a busy fight writes a line for every hit.

# Unreal and ck-exec names
Source: https://docs.crowdedkingdoms.com/unreal-sdk/exec/unreal-and-ck-exec-names

# Unreal and ck-exec names

:::note
Server Objects run on [ck-exec](/exec/intro).
:::

The SDK names things the way an Unreal project would. The platform's [ck-exec pages](/exec/intro), its operations tools and its logs use their own words. This table maps one to the other.

| Unreal SDK | ck-exec |
|---|---|
| Server Object type: one definition asset, `UCrowdyServerObjectDefinition` | hub node type |
| Type Name | node type name |
| Server Object: `UCrowdyServerObject`, from `UCrowdyServerObjectSubsystem` | a hub instance |
| Instance Id | instance key |
| Variables: the State Struct, or the variables added in the asset | the hub's state, kept in its snapshots |
| Server Function | method |
| Server Name of a function | method name |
| Calling a Server Function: `UCrowdyServerObject::Call` | a call |
| Call outcome: `ECrowdyServerCallOutcome` | reply status (mapped on [Troubleshooting](./troubleshooting.md#outcomes)) |
| Variables Visible to Players, and following them: `WatchValues` | the hub's `state` topic, subscribed to, and its `read` method |
| Server message, sent by `messages::send_...` | a topic the hub publishes on (any topic but `state`) |
| Server Name of a message | topic |
| Listening to a message: `WatchMessage` in a game, `listen::<type>::<message>` in server code | subscribing to a hub instance's topic |
| Listen To | the types in the manifest's `calls`, which may subscribe |
| Kind: Server Function Library | a spoke node type, `"kind": "spoke"` in the manifest |
| Min Instances | `replicas` |
| Max Instances | `max_replicas` |
| Parallel Calls per Instance | `concurrency` |
| Calling a library: `UCrowdyServerObjectLibrary::CallLibraryFunction`, the **Call** node with no Target | a call to the spoke with the empty key; the platform picks an instance |
| Can Call Any Type | `"calls": ["*"]`; in server code, `calls::any` over `ctx.call` |
| Save Interval Seconds | `persist_every_ms` |
| Idle Timeout Seconds | `evict_after_ms` |
| The type's server code, generated into `Server/<Type Name>/` by **Generate Server Code** | the type's crate, built into the module its manifest entry names |
| Your code in `logic.rs`, implementing `Functions` | the hub's handlers: the generated `lib.rs` implements `Hub` and calls yours. For a library, it implements `Spoke` |
| Deploy on the Server Compute page, and `-op=deploy` | a build (`execBuild`) then a deploy (`execDeploy`) of a manifest that lists every type under a `root` hub type |
| Version: one deploy, listed on the Versions tab of the Server Compute page, with **Make active** to go back | a version (`execVersions`); activating an earlier one is `execActivateVersion`, a rollback |
| Switch off and Switch on for a type | the kill switch, `execSetEnabled` with a node type; calls are refused with `Paused` meanwhile |
| A call and its log lines: click a line's flow to follow it | a flow, the 32 hex digits every line of one call carries (`execLogs`) |
| The Activity tab of the Server Compute page | `execEndpointStats`, calls per endpoint |

Mods and CLIENT halves have no Unreal SDK counterpart yet. A spoke is a [Server Function Library](./server-function-libraries.md).

Two platform names show up where you might not expect them. `read` is the method the SDK calls to fetch the watched values, which is why no Server Function may use that name. And `state` is the topic every Server Object's server code publishes its variable changes on; a message cannot use it.

- [Make a Server Function Library](./server-function-libraries.md)

# Move from Game Models
Source: https://docs.crowdedkingdoms.com/unreal-sdk/exec/move-from-game-models

# Move from Game Models

:::note
Server Objects run on [ck-exec](/exec/intro). v2.18.0 added them and deprecated the Game Model API; [v2.19.0 removes it](../guides/whats-changed.md#2026-10-12-sdk-v2190).
:::

The SDK's Game Model API is removed in v2.19.0, the release after the one that adds Server Objects. It was built on a game API engine that ck-exec replaced, so it had no server to talk to. This page says what went, what to do in your project before you upgrade, what takes the place of each part, and how to move a system across. The replacement is [Server Objects](./overview.md), from Blueprint or C++.

## What was removed

- **The Game Model API.** Containers and attributes (the `CrowdyModel` and `CrowdyContainer` metadata), model functions, Crowdy Effects (the assets, the effect graph editor and the Apply Effect nodes), sessions on the Game Model subsystem, automations, signals, pre-seeding, the Game Kit, container manifests, and `UCrowdyGameModelSubsystem`. **Get Local User Id** goes with it: use **Get User ID** on the Crowdy Game Session.
- **Its settings and logging.** The `crowdy.gamemodel.*` console variables, the `LogCrowdyGameModel` log category and the `DefaultModelNotificationCarrier` setting.
- **Server Owned in the Replication dropdown.** A Blueprint variable's **Crowdy Replication** dropdown now offers only **None** and **Replicated**.
- **CrowdyMass's Game Model values.** `GetModelValue`, `GetModelTargetState`, `GetEffectTarget` and the model fields are gone. Crowd rows read Server Object values instead, from a record per entity; see [Crowd rows](./keep-a-record-per-entity.md#crowd-rows).
- **Crowdy Studio's Game Model page.** The **Features** and **Tier-feature grants** cards that were on it are on the new **Access** page, under **Project** in the Configure group.

## Upgrade steps

Do these in order.

1. **Compile and open the project on the release that adds Server Objects first.** That release still has the Game Model API, and every use of it is listed: each C++ use gets a compiler warning (C4996 on MSVC), and each Blueprint that uses Game Models gets one compiler warning listing its uses when it compiles, loads or cooks. Write the list down, and [move each system](#move-a-system) off Game Models while the nodes are still there to read.
2. **Search your C++ for `CrowdyModel`, and for `CrowdyContainer`.** A property or Blueprint variable that still carries either marker compiles and does nothing, and nothing warns you. Remove the marker, or the property if it was only a Game Model attribute.3. **Know what the upgrade drops without a message.** A Blueprint that still has **Apply Effect** nodes loses those nodes when it loads, with no error, so step 1 is the only place they are listed. Crowdy Effect, container manifest and Game Kit assets no longer load; note what they described and delete them. An old saved `DefaultModelNotificationCarrier` is ignored and can be deleted from your config.
4. **Fix the C++ that no longer compiles** (see [the removed C++ API](#the-removed-c-api)).
5. **Do a clean cook.** Do not cook iteratively over the upgrade: the baked registry's layout changed, so rebuild it and cook from scratch. See [Packaging](../guides/packaging.md).
6. **Check your channel code.** The SDK no longer drops channel payloads that begin `cmc:`, `csg:` or `gms|`, so a payload that starts that way now reaches your handler. See [Channels](../runtime/channels.md).

## The removed C++ API

- `ICrowdyEntitySubscriber::ApplyModelChanges` is gone. A class that implements the interface and marks it `override` stops compiling; delete the function.
- `UCrowdyEntitySubsystem::RegisterSubParticipant`, `RegisterSubParticipantAs` and `DeriveSubParticipantID` are gone.
- `FCrowdyModelIdentity` is gone. `FCrowdyEntityIdentity` has `StableNetIDFromActorPath` and `NetIDFromBindingKey` for the same jobs.
- `FCrowdyEntityRecord::AnchorNetID` is gone.
- `ICrowdyBindingKeyProvider` stays. Its header now lives under `Replication/Components/`, so fix an include that names the old path.

The CrowdyState layout's message for a container property now reads "use a CrowdyEvent RPC or a Server Object" where it used to name a Game Model container; see [Crowdy State](../runtime/crowdy-state.md).

## What takes the place of each part

| Game Models | Server Objects |
|---|---|
| A container type | A Server Object definition asset: [Create a Server Object type](./create-a-type.md) |
| Container attributes (`CrowdyModel`) | The state struct's variables. What players may read is the values that are **Visible to Players**, the ones they watch: [Create a Server Object type](./create-a-type.md#the-details-tab) |
| Model functions and Effects | Server Functions, written in the type's `logic.rs`: [Write its server logic](./write-server-logic.md) |
| Invoke policies | **Callable By** and **Readable By** on the asset, and checks in the logic: [Access, members and timers](./access-members-and-timers.md#access) |
| A match session | One Server Object per match, with the match id as its Instance Id: [Relate Server Objects to each other](./relate-server-objects.md) |
| Change pings, **Listen for Model Changes**, OnRep on model attributes | Following the watched variables, from [Blueprint](./from-blueprint/read-and-follow-variables.md) or [C++](./from-cpp/read-and-follow-variables.md) |
| Automations: interval schedules | The type's timers: [Timers and events](./access-members-and-timers.md#timers-and-events) |
| Automations: cron schedules | No setting on the asset for now; the platform's [Cron schedules](/exec/timers-and-presence#cron-schedules) |
| `player_joined`, `player_left`, `player_count_changed` triggers | **On Player Joined** and **On Player Left** on the type, and presence on the server: [Presence](/exec/timers-and-presence#presence) |
| Authority rules (tier features, group and grid permissions) | A tier feature: [Required Feature](./access-members-and-timers.md#required-feature) on the function. Group and grid permissions: checks in the logic against the player and the world, [World and platform data](/exec/world-and-platform-data) |

In Oakford, had the beacon that a villager feeds with oil been a Game Model container, it would have had an `Oil` attribute and a `FeedBeacon` model function, guarded by an invoke policy. As a Server Object it is the `AVillageBeacon` type from [What a Server Object is](./overview.md): `Oil` is a variable players watch, and `FeedBeacon` is a Server Function that adds the oil or refuses.

## Move a system

Do this for each system on your list, while the project is still on the release that has both Game Models and Server Objects.

1. **Author each system as a Server Object type**: make the [definition asset](./create-a-type.md), set [who may read and call it](./access-members-and-timers.md), [write its logic](./write-server-logic.md) and [deploy it with Server Compute](./deploy-with-server-compute.md).
2. **Switch the call sites.** Read and follow values and call functions [from Blueprint](./from-blueprint/get-a-server-object.md) or [from C++](./from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md), and remove the Game Model nodes and calls as you go.
3. **Seed any data that must persist.** Nothing moves automatically. A one-off script writes the starting values into the new type, for example by calling a [Server Only](./create-a-type.md#callable-by) Server Function, which developer tools can call and players cannot.

Server Objects need ck-exec on your app's environment, so a project can finish moving once its environment has it.

## Why Server Objects are not marked on the class

Game Models were declared by markers on your own classes. Server Objects are declared in one asset, on purpose:

- **The truth is the server code.** A property on an actor that looks writable is only a request to the server. Keeping the state in the server code makes that plain.
- **A Server Object is not an actor.** It is picked by an Instance Id, exists before any actor does and outlives them, and many actors can share one.
- **One versioned contract.** The asset is the single place the type is described, so compiling a Blueprint can never silently change what the server expects.
- **Marker metadata is stripped when a game is cooked,** so a property marker is not something a packaged game can read back.
- **A call answers or refuses plainly,** with an outcome and a reason, which an OnRep on an attribute cannot.

# Get a Server Object
Source: https://docs.crowdedkingdoms.com/unreal-sdk/exec/from-blueprint/get-a-server-object

# Get a Server Object

:::note
Server Objects run on [ck-exec](/exec/intro).
:::

Everything on the [C++ pages](../from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md) can be done from Blueprint, and most of it needs no variable, no cast and no setup of your own. Open any Blueprint graph, type the name of a variable or function from a [definition asset](../create-a-type.md), and pick the node that appears. The node reads the variable, tells you when it changes, or calls the function, with a real pin for every value. A Blueprint and a C++ class can use the same Server Object at the same time.

To build one from nothing, following each click, see [Tip jar: your first Server Object](../examples/tip-jar.md).

## The typed nodes

Type a variable's name in the graph's palette or in the menu that opens when you drag off a pin, and the asset offers its nodes under **Server Objects**, then the asset's name. For the village beacon's `CSO_VillageBeacon` the category is **CSO Village Beacon**:

![The Palette filtered to CSO_VillageBeacon, offering Call FeedBeacon, Get bLit, Get Oil, Get Server State, On bLit Changed and On Oil Changed](/img/unreal-sdk/server-object-palette.png)

| Node | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Get Oil (CSO_VillageBeacon)** | Reads the variable `Oil`. A pure node: it has no execution pins. |
| **On Oil Changed (CSO_VillageBeacon)** | Runs when `Oil` changes. |
| **Call FeedBeacon (CSO_VillageBeacon)** | Calls the function `FeedBeacon`, with a pin for each input and each output. |
| **Get Server State (CSO_VillageBeacon)** | Every variable of the object at once, one output pin each. |

[Blueprint snippet: so-typed-nodes, see /bp/unreal-sdk/so-typed-nodes.txt]

Pan a Blueprint figure with the right mouse button. Press **Copy nodes**, then Ctrl+V in your own event graph. The figure shows the four nodes for `Oil`; `bLit` has a **Get** and an **On bLit Changed** of its own, as the palette shows.

There is one **Get** and one **On Changed** for each variable and one **Call** for each function of the asset, and one **On Received** for each message players can listen to; see [Hear its messages](./hear-server-messages.md). Only variables ticked **Visible to Players** are offered, since a **Server Only** variable never reaches a player. There is also a generic **Call Server Function** under **Server Objects**, with a **Function** dropdown that lists every function of every asset, for when you would rather pick than type.

A [Server Function Library](../server-function-libraries.md) is different: it has no values and no instance, so its only nodes are **Call** nodes, under **Server Function Libraries** in the palette, and they need no **Target**; see [Call a Server Function Library](./call-a-library.md).

There is no bookkeeping to do. A Server Object is one shared object that the SDK keeps current. **Get** reads that object's current value directly, never a copy you have to refresh. **On Changed** follows it, so you do not keep a variable holding the last value, compare it, or unbind anything. Rename or retype a variable in the asset and the nodes follow; see [When the asset changes](./pins-for-every-type.md#when-the-asset-changes).

## Where the object comes from

Every typed node needs a Server Object. There are three ways to give it one.

- **Target.** The default. The **Target** pin takes the Server Object, a **Crowdy Server Object** component, or an actor that has a component for that asset. Left empty it is **Self**, so a node in a Blueprint that has the component just works. Anything else cannot be connected to it, and the editor says why.
- **Find By Asset.** For a widget or other Blueprint with no reference to pass in. Right-click the node and choose **Find By Asset**; the **Target** pin is replaced by the choice of **Instance**, which you can also change in the node's Details.
  - **Instance Id**: a pin takes the id, such as `oakford`.
  - **Signed-In Player**: the signed-in player's own object, for an [Owner Only](../from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md#owner-only-types) type.
  - **Player's Team**: the signed-in player's [Crowdy Team](../access-members-and-timers.md#crowdy-team). A **Team Id** pin picks the team when the player is in several; 0 uses the first.

  In C++ the choice of **Instance** is the enum `ECrowdyServerObjectFind`, with the values `InstanceId`, `SignedInPlayer` and `PlayersTeam`.

  The object is acquired the first time a node of this Blueprint uses it, and held while the Blueprint lives. Right-click the node and choose **Use Target** to go back.
- **Only One Instance.** A type with [Only One Instance](../access-members-and-timers.md#only-one-instance) has just the one object, so its nodes need neither a Target nor an Instance. Place the node and use it.

## Add the component

The typed nodes take **Self** as the default **Target**, so the simplest way to have a Server Object is an actor with a component. Open the Blueprint actor, click **Add** in the Components panel, and choose **Crowdy Server Object**. In its Details panel, under **Server Object**:

- **Definition**: the definition asset, such as the `CSO_VillageBeacon` from [Create a Server Object type](../create-a-type.md).
- **Instance Mode**: which Server Object of that type this actor uses. A type with Only One Instance ignores it.
  - **Instance Id**: the id typed in **Instance Id**. Every actor with the same id shares one Server Object. The beacon uses the village's name, `oakford`.
  - **Signed-In Player**: the signed-in player's user id. Use it for an [Owner Only](../from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md#owner-only-types) type, so each player gets their own. The component waits for the player to sign in, and joins again after a new sign-in or a new account.
  - **This Actor**: the actor's placement in the level, which is the same on every player's machine. Only for an actor placed in the level with the component already on it, not one spawned at run time or given the component at run time.
  - **Player's Team**: the signed-in player's [Crowdy Team](../access-members-and-timers.md#crowdy-team), for a type whose **Members From** is **Crowdy Team**. **Team Id** picks the team; 0 uses the player's only team. The component gets the player's teams if the game has not, and joins again when **On My Teams Changed** runs. A player in several teams fails with "This player is in 2 teams; set Team Id": set **Team Id**, then call **Rejoin**.
  - **This Actor's Area**: the Server Object of the area the actor stands in. The ground is cut into squares of the definition's **Area Size** chunks on each side, and the Instance Id is the square's `x,y`. The component checks every half second and, when the actor crosses into another area, joins that area's object and lets go of the old one. For a type that keeps [a record per entity](../keep-a-record-per-entity.md#pick-the-object), the actor also needs a **Crowdy Entity** component, since its id names the actor's record. Needs a game session, which gives the chunk size. In C++ the mode is `ECrowdyServerObjectInstanceMode::ThisActorsArea`.
  - **From Server Value**: the Instance Id is a variable of another Server Object, followed as it changes. Set **Source Definition**, **Source Instance** (the enum `ECrowdyServerObjectSourceInstance`: **Instance Id**, with **Source Instance Id**, or **Signed-In Player**) and **Source Variable**, a String or an integer. While the variable is empty the component waits ("Waiting for TeamId"), and when it changes the component joins the new one. See [Guild Halls](../examples/guild-halls-and-arenas.md#guild-halls).

![The Crowdy Server Object component: Definition CSO_VillageBeacon, Instance Mode Instance Id, Instance Id oakford](/img/unreal-sdk/server-object-component.png)

The component joins at Begin Play and lets go at End Play. The Server Object is given back a few seconds after its last holder lets go, so a beacon that is destroyed and placed again straight away keeps its values. See [Get a Server Object](../from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md#one-object-many-owners).

When the player's access to the game ends, the Server Object fails and its **Get Failure Reason** says why. After the player signs in again, the component, like a typed node set to **Find By Asset**, gets its Server Object again on its own; you do not call **Rejoin**. Show the reason from **On Access Ended**, which [Authentication](../../services/authentication.md#when-the-players-access-ends) covers.

If you change **Definition** or **Instance Id** in a graph after the actor has begun play, call **Rejoin** on the component. It also tries again after a failure. While the component is joining, Rejoin does nothing, so calling it from the component's own **On Status Changed** cannot loop.

### Its events and nodes

| Event or node | What it does |
|---|---|
| **On Variables Changed** (event) | Runs after every change of the Variables players can see, and once when they are first read. It gives the Server Object and the names that changed. The delegate is `FCrowdyServerVariablesChanged`. |
| **On Status Changed** (event) | Runs when the Server Object's status changes. **Object** is None when it could not be joined. The delegate is `FCrowdyServerStatusChanged`, which gives the Server Object and its status. |
| **Get Server Object** | The Server Object the component holds, or None before it joins one or after it could not. |
| **Get Failure Reason** | Why there is no usable Server Object, or empty. |
| **Rejoin** | Joins again. |

## Without the component

The component is a convenience over the same nodes. You can use them from any Blueprint, such as a widget that shows the beacon's oil without owning it. A widget needs no component for this: either use a typed node with **Find By Asset**, or call **Get Server Object** with the widget as the **Owner** and connect the result to the typed nodes' **Target**. These nodes, and **Set Server Value** and **Get Server Value**, are in the function library `UCrowdyServerObjectLibrary`:

- **Get Server Object**: takes a **Definition**, an **Instance Id** and an **Owner** (which defaults to the Blueprint itself), and returns the Server Object, or None with **Error** saying why. Owners that ask for the same one share it. It is held until the owner is destroyed.
- **Release Server Object**: stops one owner holding it, for an owner that lives on after it stops needing it, such as a widget that is reused.
- **Get Player Instance Id**: the signed-in player's user id, which is the Instance Id of their own [Owner Only](../from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md#owner-only-types) object. It is empty when nobody is signed in.

On the Server Object itself:

| Node | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Get Status** | Connecting, Ready, Failed or Released. See [Status](../from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md#status). |
| **Get Failure Reason** | Why it Failed, or what it is waiting for. |
| **Get Instance Id** | The Instance Id it was joined with. |
| **Get Definition** | The definition asset the object was made from, to pass to nodes that take one. A pure node. |
| **On Status Changed** | An event that runs when the status changes. |

The statuses are the ones from C++; see [Status](../from-cpp/get-a-server-object.md#status).

# Read and follow its variables
Source: https://docs.crowdedkingdoms.com/unreal-sdk/exec/from-blueprint/read-and-follow-variables

# Read and follow its variables

:::note
Server Objects run on [ck-exec](/exec/intro).
:::

Players see the variables their [definition](../create-a-type.md) marks **Visible to Players**. The typed nodes read them and follow their changes, each with a real pin of the variable's type. The examples use the village beacon, whose `CSO_VillageBeacon` asset has `Oil`, `bLit` and a Server Only `LastFedBy`. Every node here needs a Server Object; see [Get a Server Object](./get-a-server-object.md#where-the-object-comes-from).

## Get a variable

**Get Oil** has one output pin, **Oil**, typed as the variable is. It reads the object's current value each time the node is used. Before the server has sent the values it reads the variable's default from the asset. A **Get** with nothing behind it, such as a **Target** that holds no object for that asset, gives the default too.

To tell a real zero from "the server has not answered yet", use the node's advanced pin, **Oil Has Value**. It is collapsed by default: click the small arrow at the bottom of the node to show it. It is false until the server has sent this Server Object's values, and true after. A variable that is an optional in C++ has a **Has Value** pin that is always shown, and it is false when the optional is empty or the values have not arrived; see [What the pins are](./pins-for-every-type.md#what-the-pins-are).

**Get Server State** is the same for every visible variable at once, with one advanced **Has Values** pin that is false until the server has sent the values. It is not offered for a Server Object whose State has no variable visible to players, such as the Game Kit `CSO_Kit_Npcs`; a **Get Server State** already placed on one fails to compile with a message saying so.

The nodes work whether the definition takes its variables from a struct or you [added them in the asset](../create-a-type.md#variables-inputs-and-outputs-or-a-struct) (the List form): **Get**, **Get Server State** and **On Changed** read and follow a variable added in the asset with the same pins.

## Follow a variable

**On Oil Changed** is for an event graph. It has a **Bind** execution pin in, **Then** and **Changed** execution pins out, and the value as an output pin. Wire **Bind** from **Begin Play** once:

```text
Event BeginPlay -> On Oil Changed (Bind)
                     Changed -> Set Text (Oil)
```

- **Changed** runs right away with the current value as soon as the object is ready, and again after every change of that variable, and only of that variable. A Game Kit starter's **On Changed** and **On Variables Changed** run once when it is Ready, not also before: a snapshot pushed while it is still connecting does not announce.
- Each **On Changed** node you place is its own binding, so you can use the same variable's node more than once in one graph: bind one from **Begin Play** and another from a custom event, and each runs **Changed** once per change.
- Run the same node's **Bind** again, for example with another **Target**, and it replaces its own binding; it does not run twice. It runs **Changed** once at once with the current value when the object is Ready.
- There is nothing to unbind. A binding goes away when the Blueprint that owns it is destroyed or the Server Object is given back.
- Through a component or an actor it follows whatever object that component joins. If the player's team changes and the component joins another team's object, **Changed** runs with the new object's value.
- A node whose **Bind** is not connected never runs, so the compile gives a warning.
- Bound to something that is not a Server Object of that asset, nothing is watched and the log says so.

## Show the oil

The village square's beacon, `BP_VillageBeacon`, has a Crowdy Server Object component with **Definition** set to `CSO_VillageBeacon`, **Instance Mode** on **Instance Id**, and **Instance Id** set to `oakford`. In its Event Graph:

1. Add **On Oil Changed (CSO_VillageBeacon)** and wire **Event BeginPlay** into its **Bind**.
2. From **Changed**, use **Oil**, for example to set a text or a light's intensity. The figure sends it through a conversion to a **Print String**. It runs once when the object is ready, and again after every change, so this one graph covers both.
3. For the lamp, add **On bLit Changed (CSO_VillageBeacon)** from the **Then** pin of the first node, and wire its **bLit** to **Set Visibility** on the light, `Light` in the figure.

[Blueprint snippet: so-show-oil, see /bp/unreal-sdk/so-show-oil.txt]

Pan a Blueprint figure with the right mouse button. Press **Copy nodes**, then Ctrl+V in your own event graph.

Anywhere else in the graph, **Get Oil (CSO_VillageBeacon)** gives the current amount. `LastFedBy` is Server Only, so it has no nodes here.

## A widget that shows the oil

A widget has no component, so use **Find By Asset**. In its Event Construct, add **On Oil Changed (CSO_VillageBeacon)**, right-click it, choose **Find By Asset**, leave **Instance** on **Instance Id** and type `oakford` into its **Instance Id** pin. Wire Construct into **Bind**, and **Changed** into **SetText** on the widget's `OilText`, with **To Text** turning the **Oil** into text. The widget holds the beacon while it lives.

[Blueprint snippet: so-widget-oil, see /bp/unreal-sdk/so-widget-oil.txt]

## How many players are online

Every app has one root Server Object, which Server Compute deploys along with your types. It counts the players in the app's world. **Get Players Online** reads that count:

- It takes an **Owner**, the Blueprint itself unless you connect another object, and gives **Players Online** and a return value that is false until the count first arrives.
- The first call starts following the count, and the owner keeps it followed until the owner is destroyed. So a widget can read it in a binding, or an actor on Tick.
- The count is the number of players the platform's realtime servers report for your app. A player who leaves is still counted for a few minutes, until their session ends.

The root's definition is `CSO_PlayersOnline`, in the Crowdy SDK's content under **Data**. Use it like any other definition, for example with **Find By Asset** on the **On Changed** node for **PlayersOnline**, to run a graph each time the count changes. Leave the asset as it is: deploying sends the root's server code as the SDK writes it.

A project with the Game Kit's `world` starter has `world` as its root instead, and **Get Players Online** reads the world's `Online` variable, from the definition **Game Kit World** in Project Settings names (`CSO_Kit_World`, set when you add the starter). See [The world becomes the app's root](../use-game-kit-starters.md#the-world-becomes-the-apps-root). If the world's snapshot carries no player count, as a world deployed from the platform's own starter pack does not, **Get Players Online** returns false, with 0, for good, and the log says why once.

An app last deployed with an older Crowdy SDK, or never deployed from Server Compute, has no Crowdy SDK root. Deploy once from Server Compute. Until then **Get Players Online** returns false, and the log says why once for each reason in each game instance (so once per Play In Editor client): "This app has no Crowdy SDK root, so Players Online has no count: deploy the app from Server Compute (an app last deployed with an older Crowdy SDK, or by another tool, has none). It is asked again every minute." The root waits and asks again once a minute instead of every few seconds, and once the app is deployed the count arrives without restarting the game.

## Records

A type whose **Holds** is **A Record per Entity** keeps its variables once for each entity; see [Keep a record per entity](../keep-a-record-per-entity.md). A component on an entity's actor reads that actor's own record, so everything above works unchanged. **Get**, **On Changed**, **On Variables Changed** and **Get Server Value** read the record, and a variable the player may not receive reads its default and never changes.

To read the other records, take the Server Object from the component with **Get Server Object**. On it:

- **Find Record** takes an **Id** and gives that record's **Values**, its **Owner** (a user id, 0 for none) and its **Team**. It returns false when there is no such record. Read a variable out of **Values** with **Get Server Value**.
- **Get Record Ids** gives the id of every record the player can see, in no particular order.
- **Holds Records** says whether the type keeps records, and **Num Records** counts them.

A Game Kit starter whose hub keeps a collection, such as the world's resource nodes, holds its members as records too, read with the same nodes on its Server Object; see [Its records](../use-game-kit-starters.md#use-it-from-blueprint-and-c).
- **Watch Record** takes a **Record Id** and an event (the delegate `FCrowdyServerRecordEvent`), which runs with the **Object**, the **Record Id** and the **Changed** variables after each change of that record and when it is removed (**Find Record** is then false). If the record is already current it also runs once at once, naming all its variables. A watch added from an **On Records Changed** or **On Records Updated** handler gets that catch-up and does not run a second time for the same change. **Stop Watching Record** removes it. Records dropped because the object **Failed** are not reported; **On Status Changed** is.
- **On Records Changed** is an event. Bind it with **Assign** on the Server Object. It runs after every read, batch or fetch that changed records, with the **Object**, the ids that are new or changed (**Changed Ids**) and the ids that were removed (**Removed Ids**).
- **On Records Updated** is bound the same way and runs at the same times, but gives a list of **Record Id** with its **Changed Variables**, then the removed ids. **Changed Variables** is empty when only the record's owner or team changed.

Ids are compared with capitals significant. **Find By Asset**, and **Watch Variables** on a Server Object of this kind, read its defaults and not a record: use the component or **Find Record**.

## By name

The typed nodes cover a Server Object whose shape you know. The by-name nodes work by name and by type, for the dynamic cases: a graph that shows any variable by a name in a data table, or one that works for several types. They are the ones every Blueprint had before typed nodes, and they still work.

### Show the oil by name

Select the component and add its **On Variables Changed** event. The event runs once when the Variables are first read and again after each change, so one graph covers both:

1. From **Object**, call **Get Variables**.
2. Call **Get Server Value** on that, with **Name** set to `Oil`. Its **Value** pin takes the type of whatever you connect to it, here an Integer.
3. Use the value, for example to set a text or a light's intensity. `bLit` reads the same way, into a Boolean.

**Get Server Value** returns false when the Variables have no value by that name or it is of another type. Names are matched ignoring case, spaces and punctuation, so `Max Health` and `maxhealth` find the same Variable, in the editor and in a packaged game. A C++ `float` Variable reads into a Blueprint Float. A Variable that is **Server Only** is never sent to players, so it always reads its default here.

### The nodes for reading and watching

| Node | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Get Variables** | The Variables the server last sent, to read with **Get Server Value**. They hold their defaults until the object is Ready. |
| **Watch Variables** | Takes an event (the delegate `FCrowdyServerVariablesEvent`) and runs it after every change, with the names that changed. If the Variables are already current it also runs once at once, naming them all. |
| **Stop Watching Variables** | Removes an event that **Watch Variables** was given. |
| **Get Members** | The user ids of the members, in the order they joined. Only for a type whose **Members From** is **This Object** with **Show Members to Players** on; empty otherwise. |
| **Get Member Count** | How many members there are, even when the list is not shown. |
| **Get Leader** | The leader's user id, or 0 when there is none. |
| **Is Open For Joining** | Whether **Join** is accepted. |
| **Is Member** | Whether the signed-in player is a member. |
| **Is Leader** | Whether the signed-in player is the leader. |

The member nodes answer for a type with [members](../access-members-and-timers.md#members). **Get Members**, **Get Member Count**, **Get Leader** and **Is Open For Joining** are for members the Server Object keeps itself; **Is Member** and **Is Leader** also work for a **Crowdy Team**. With the list shown, **Is Member** and **Is Leader** follow it and the signed-in user id. Otherwise a successful **Join** or **Leave** makes the object read again, and each read sets both.

**On Variables Changed** and **Watch Variables** name a change of these too: `Members`, `MemberCount`, `Leader` and `OpenForJoining`, so a lobby's list refreshes when someone joins.

A widget that only shows the oil by name would call **Get Server Object** in its Construct event, bind **Watch Variables** to a custom event, and read `Oil` there. It needs no component.

Two things to know about the by-name nodes:

- **Set Server Value** and **Get Server Value** work by name and by type. A misspelled name or a wrong type gives false, not an error, so branch on the result while you are wiring a graph. The typed nodes have no such failure: a wrong name or type does not compile.
- The names **On Variables Changed** and **Watch Variables** give are the ones **Get Server Value** takes, the variable's own name in the asset, even when the definition's **Server Names** gives a Variable a different name on the server.

# Hear its messages
Source: https://docs.crowdedkingdoms.com/unreal-sdk/exec/from-blueprint/hear-server-messages

# Hear its messages

:::note
Server Objects run on [ck-exec](/exec/intro).
:::

A message is the server telling everyone listening that something happened, such as the Hollow Giant falling. The type's [definition](../create-a-type.md#server-messages) lists its messages, and its [server code](../write-server-logic.md#send-a-message) sends them. A game hears one with a typed node, **On Message Received**, or with **Watch Message** when it has to work by name. Every node here needs a Server Object; see [Get a Server Object](./get-a-server-object.md#where-the-object-comes-from).

A message is an event, not a value. **Received** runs when the server sends the message and not at any other time: not when the object becomes ready, and not for a message sent before the game was listening. To show what is true now, such as whether the boss is defeated, read a variable with **Get** and **On Changed**; see [Read and follow its variables](./read-and-follow-variables.md).

## Hear a message

**On BossDefeated Received (CSO_Boss)** has a **Bind** execution pin in, **Then** and **Received** execution pins out, and one output pin for each value the message carries: `Winner`, an Integer64, and `Hits`, an Integer. Wire **Bind** from **Begin Play** once:

```text
Event BeginPlay -> On BossDefeated Received (Bind)
                     Received -> Print String (Winner, Hits)
```

- **Received** runs once for each message the server sends, with that message's values on the output pins.
- Each **On Received** node you place is its own binding, so you can use the same message's node more than once in one graph, and each runs **Received** once per message.
- Run the same node's **Bind** again, for example with another **Target**, and it replaces its own binding; it does not run twice.
- There is nothing to unbind. A binding goes away when the Blueprint that owns it is destroyed or the Server Object is given back.
- Through a component or an actor it follows whatever object that component joins.
- A node whose **Bind** is not connected never runs, so the compile gives a warning. Bound to something that is not a Server Object of that asset, nothing is heard and the log says so.
- It takes the object the way **On Changed** does: **Target**, the actor's component, or **Find By Asset**; see [Where the object comes from](./get-a-server-object.md#where-the-object-comes-from).

The palette offers a node for each message whose **Players Can Listen** is ticked and whose payload values all have a pin; see [Pins for every type](./pins-for-every-type.md). A message with no values has a node with **Received** and no value pins.

## Announce the fall

The boss actor `BP_Boss` from [Shared boss fight](../examples/shared-boss.md#the-blueprint) has a Crowdy Server Object component with **Definition** set to `CSO_Boss`. In its Event Graph:

1. Add **On BossDefeated Received (CSO_Boss)**. Wire its **Bind** from the **Then** pin of the last **On Changed** node you added, or from **Event BeginPlay** if it is the first.
2. From **Received**, add a **Print String** that builds the line with **Build String**: the **Winner** pin, " felled the Hollow Giant in ", the **Hits** pin and " hits".
3. Compile and save.

The figure turns **Winner** into a string first, since it is an Integer64, and builds the line from it.

[Blueprint snippet: so-boss-defeated, see /bp/unreal-sdk/so-boss-defeated.txt]

Pan a Blueprint figure with the right mouse button. Press **Copy nodes**, then Ctrl+V in your own event graph.

Play with two players, as on that page. When the boss falls, both windows print the line once, with the same **Winner**. A player who joins a moment later sees the boss already **Defeated** through **On Phase Changed**, and prints nothing: the message is gone.

If the node is not in the palette, check that the message is ticked **Players Can Listen** in the asset and that you have saved it. If the graph fails to compile with "heard only by other Server Object types; turn on Players Can Listen", the message was ticked once and is not now. If it says the asset has "no message ... any more", the message was renamed or removed: place the node again from the menu, or give the message its old name back.

## When a message is heard

The game listens to a message while a node or a **Watch Message** wants it and the connection is open. When the last one goes away it stops listening, and it starts again after a dropped connection comes back.

- **A message that arrives while the object is reading its values is held.** It runs after the values are current, so a graph that reads the variables from **Received** sees the state the message followed. At most 32 are held; past that the oldest is dropped and the log warns.
- **A message is announced only while the Server Object is Ready.** One that arrives while it is Connecting is held until it is.
- **A message sent while the connection is closed is lost.** Nothing is replayed when it comes back; the game reads the variables again, and **On Changed** reports what differs, but a message is not a value and cannot be read again.
- **A message in a record type can arrive before the record change it follows.** A type that keeps [a record per entity](../keep-a-record-per-entity.md) sends its records in batches, so a message sent right after a record changed may be heard before that record shows the change. Put what the listener needs into the payload, or read the record when the next batch arrives.
- **A refused listen is asked again.** If the server refuses to let the game listen to a message, the log warns once with the platform's reason and the game asks again after a wait that grows from 1 second to 30. Nothing else about the Server Object fails.
- **Every message listened to is a subscription.** A connection allows 256 subscriptions in all, and each subscribe counts against the 120 calls a connection may make every 10 seconds. A game that listens to a few messages on a few Server Objects never gets near either; see [A message never arrives](../troubleshooting.md#a-message-never-arrives).

## By name

The typed nodes cover a message you know. **Watch Message** and **Stop Watching Message** work by name, for a graph that listens to a message from a data table, or to one of several assets. Both are on the Server Object itself, so get it first with **Get Server Object** or from a component.

| Node | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Watch Message** | Takes a **Message**, the message's Name, and an event (the delegate `FCrowdyServerMessageEvent`), and runs the event each time the server sends that message. The event gives the **Object**, the **Message** and the **Payload**. |
| **Stop Watching Message** | Removes an event that **Watch Message** was given. |

Read the values from **Payload** with **Get Server Value**, as you would read the variables:

1. Call **Get Server Object** in the actor's or widget's start event, and from its result call **Watch Message** with **Message** set to `BossDefeated`.
2. Drag from the **Event** pin and choose **Add Custom Event**, named `OnBossMessage`.
3. In the event, call **Get Server Value** on **Payload** with **Name** set to `Winner`, into an Integer64, and again for `Hits`.

The first figure is steps 1 and 2: **Watch Message** on the component's Server Object, and the custom event wired to its **Event** pin. The second is step 3, where the event reads both values from its **Payload** and prints the same line as the typed node.

[Blueprint snippet: so-watch-message, see /bp/unreal-sdk/so-watch-message.txt]

[Blueprint snippet: so-message-payload, see /bp/unreal-sdk/so-message-payload.txt]

The same rules hold as for the typed node. Nothing runs for a message sent before you watched. Watching the same event twice runs it once. **Stop Watching Message** removes it, and an event whose Blueprint is destroyed stops running by itself. It takes the same **Message** and the same event that **Watch Message** was given:

[Blueprint snippet: so-unwatch-message, see /bp/unreal-sdk/so-unwatch-message.txt]

Watching a name the definition does not have, or one whose **Players Can Listen** is off, does nothing: the log warns "CSO_Boss has no message named ... so nothing can listen to it", or "... is heard only by other Server Object types; turn on Players Can Listen to hear it in a game", and the event never runs. The by-name nodes check at run time, not when you compile, so test the graph once. **Get Server Value** returns false when **Payload** has no value by that name or of that type; see [By name](./read-and-follow-variables.md#by-name).
